title: Banasura Vadham
body:
Banasura Vadham

Banasura was the powerful king of Sonitpur, in the land of modern-day Assam, and an ardent devotee of Lord Shiva. Pleased with his intense penance, Shiva had blessed him with a thousand arms and personally assured him of protection in any battle. In his devotion Banasura used each of his thousand arms to play a different instrument for the Lord — the mridangam, celestial bells, the veena, conch shells — and whenever Shiva performed His Tandava dance, Banasura would accompany Him with a thousand instruments in perfect harmony. But with this boon Banasura grew arrogant, and longed for a worthy opponent to prove his might.
Banasura had a beautiful daughter, Usha, a devoted worshipper of Devi Parvati. Pleased with her devotion, the Goddess appeared to her and foretold that the man who would appear in her dreams would be her destined husband. One night Usha dreamed of a prince of unmatched radiance, with broad shoulders and a slender waist, coral-like lips, a face like a lotus, and eyes that shone like the sun and the moon. She confided in her friend Chitralekha, an artist gifted with the power to draw the perfect likeness of anyone described to her, and as Usha described the man, Chitralekha sketched him. Comparing the drawing to the princes and warriors of Bharata, the two discovered that the man was Aniruddha, the grandson of Shri Krishna.
Chitralekha possessed another power — she could teleport to any place and bring back whomever she wished. That very night, at Usha's request, she carried the sleeping Aniruddha from Dwaraka to Usha's chambers in Sonitpur, unseen, for her father was a sworn enemy of Krishna. For days the two lived in secret, until rumors reached Banasura. Enraged, he stormed into his daughter's chambers, found Aniruddha there, and bound him with a thousand serpents, then sent word to Dwaraka boasting of what he had done and daring anyone to rescue the prince.
When the news reached Dwaraka, Krishna and Balarama set out at once for Sonitpur on Garuda with their army, and upon arrival demanded that Aniruddha be released and Usha given to him in marriage. Banasura refused and commanded his army to attack, but Krishna and Balarama crushed his forces with ease. Seeing his army in ruins, Banasura invoked the protection of Lord Shiva, who first sent his Ganas and then came himself to face Krishna. The duel between them was fierce, a cosmic clash that shook the heavens: Shiva hurled his trident, and Krishna shattered it with His mace; Shiva loosed celestial arrows, and Krishna answered with a shield of divine energy and arrows that shone like the sun. Shiva invoked a weapon of great destruction, and Krishna countered with the Vaishnava Astra; and when Shiva at last released the Rudra-Jwaram, a deadly plague, Krishna answered with the cooling Vaishnava-Jwaram, an antidote that neutralized the affliction. Meanwhile Balarama faced Kartikeya, the son of Shiva, and struck him down.
Now bereft of all protection, Banasura stood exposed, and Krishna sent His Sudarshana Chakra after him. The discus pursued him relentlessly and, as he fled, severed nine hundred and ninety-six of his thousand arms, leaving him utterly humiliated. Defeated and stripped of his arrogance, Banasura fell at Krishna's feet and pleaded for mercy. Krishna, ever compassionate, spared his life on the condition that he surrender to dharma. Banasura released Aniruddha and gladly agreed to his marriage with Usha, and so, with peace restored, the two were united, fulfilling the prophecy of Devi Parvati.
